superficial: A slate plaque, polished by the hand of whoever passed it every day. At the top, in large letters: "ENCLOSURE OF CAPTURE. First ring".
Below it, the motto of the works: "What the star gives, the star will pay for".
Lower down, the delivery date, carved and empty. And the signature of the Transit Council, in full: seven signs, the last one struck out.
A blackboard with two columns, half rubbed out. On the left: "Estimated completion of the Enclosure: forty years". On the right: "Estimated time until the network collapses: nine".
Someone has circled the nine twice in chalk. Beside it, in another hand: "What if we calculated wrong?".
No one has written below it. The chalk is still on the ledge, worn down to a fingertip.
A huge dish looks up at the Ember from its mast. One edge still wears the building tarpaulin: it never received its light in full.
A copper counter tallies the energy captured. It reads almost zero.
The cables run down to a knot of connections marked with the sign of the network of Gates. The energy was not meant for a house or a factory: it was going to feed the Gates.
A building-site notebook, its corners black from handling. The last pages have hardly any figures.
"Day 3,211. The Council orders the cranes stopped. The notice says the deadline can't be met, as if we had only found out today".
"Day 3,212. They send all of us to the Gates. I leave the key in. If anyone finishes this, may they finish it better than we did".
Minutes of the Transit Council, in full, with a single item: the choice. Two petitions lie on the table.
The first, from the researcher: the resources to finish her device, and not to evacuate through the Gates meanwhile. The second, the Enclosure's, which promises energy "enough to cover any debt".
The second is approved. Six signs, and a seventh struck out.
In the margin, in pencil, unsigned: "Debt is not paid with energy. It is paid with time".
